Okay, the user just said “nothing else should be using my GPU. could be old runs”. I’ve already killed the stray processes that were hogging the GPU (the extra train.py and pytest). After that, the GPU appears free (nvidia‑smi shows no compute apps). So the immediate problem of GPU contention is resolved.

Now I need to get the training back on track. Earlier diagnostics showed that the STM (self‑training module) was dying with NaN losses and eventually the whole run was killed. The checkpoint inspection revealed that the main training run (the one in `runs/20260611_172728`) has reasonable loss values up to step 30 000, so the core model training seems okay. However, the `git status` output shows a bunch of modified files: several modules under `src/mythosmini` and also `train.py`. The `git diff --stat` gave a summary: changes in `optimizer.py`, `sft.py`, `stm.py`, and `train.py`. The subsequent `git diff` snippets only showed tiny additions (e.g., a single “+” line in `__init__.py`), but the real substantive changes are in those four files.

Since the STM component is the one that produced NaNs and caused the OOM reductions, I should examine what modifications were made to `src/mythosmini/training/stm.py`. Likewise, the optimizer and SFT (supervised fine‑tuning) modules may have been altered in ways that affect loss computation or gradient scaling, potentially introducing NaNs. The `train.py` script itself may have been edited to change how runs are launched or how checkpoints are saved, which could also influence the failure.

The next logical step is to look at the actual code differences for these suspect files. I already have a `git diff` command that can show the changes, but I need to include all relevant files in one call to avoid multiple round‑trips. I’ll request a diff that includes `train.py` and the three training modules (`stm.py`, `sft.py`, `optimizer.py`). I’ll also add the transformer model file (`src/mythosmini/model/transformer.py`) just in case there were changes there that impact the forward pass and could lead to NaNs. I’ll pipe the output through `head -80` to get a reasonable chunk of the diff without overwhelming the console.

Thus, the appropriate tool call is a Bash command that runs `git diff` on those files, redirects errors to `/dev/null` (in case any file isn’t tracked), and limits the output. This will give me the concrete modifications that might be causing the STM NaNs and allow me to propose a fix.

Now I’ll issue that tool call.
